We discuss fault tolerance techniques that are used in stream processing engines that were state of the art at the time of writing (2016), namely S4, Storm, Flink, Spark Streaming, Samza and MillWheel. Further, we give insight on fault tolerance approaches that we categorize as active replication, passive replication and upstream backup. Finally, we discuss implications of the fault tolerance techniques for different streaming application requirements. This revised version corrects errors in the original 2016 manuscript, summarizes later developments in Flink and Spark, discusses durable logs and archival storage for replay, and points to more recent surveys.

papers.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
papers.summary: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.

papers.title: Dual-Mode Wireless Devices for Adaptive Pull and Push-Based Communication
papers.summary: This paper introduces a dual-mode communication framework for wireless devices that integrates query-driven (pull) and event-driven (push) transmissions within a unified time-frame structure. Devices typically respond to information requests in pull mode, but if an anomaly is detected, they preempt the regular response to report the critical condition. Additionally, push-based communication is used to proactively send critical data without waiting for a request. This adaptive approach ensures timely, context-aware, and efficient data delivery across different network conditions. To achieve high energy efficiency, we incorporate a wake-up radio mechanism and we design a tailored medium access control (MAC) protocol that supports data traffic belonging to the different communication classes. A comprehensive system-level analysis is conducted, accounting for the wake-up control operation and evaluating three key performance metrics: the success probability of anomaly reports (push traffic), the success probability of query responses (pull traffic) and the total energy consumption. Numerical results characterize the system's behavior and highlight the inherent trade-off between push and pull success probabilities as a function of allocated communication resources. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves up to a 42% reduction in energy consumption per served packet compared to traditional approaches, while maintaining reliable support for both communication paradigms.

papers.title: From Crawled to Published: A Publisher-Controlled Web Architecture for an AI-Native Internet
papers.summary: AI agents, not humans, are becoming the web's primary consumers, yet the web still ships content structured for human browsing, with no native way for publishers to expose the semantic units within it. Access is therefore mediated by a handful of AI providers that crawl, chunk, and index content unilaterally, leaving publishers little control over how their content is represented, retrieved, or attributed. We argue this is a structural problem, not one better chunking or retrieval algorithms can solve. The web lacks a native layer for publisher-controlled semantic discovery and retrieval. We propose AISTRAL, an AI-Native Internet architecture that supplies this layer. Publishers expose semantically meaningful units (e.g., passages, claims, tables) through explicit, policy-governed interfaces they control, and a web-native semantic resolver, analogous to DNS but operating over meaning rather than location, lets agents discover relevant sources before retrieving fine-grained content directly from publishers. Our end-to-end prototype matches or exceeds representative centralized retrieval pipelines in answer quality, with up to 4.2x higher accuracy on large, specialized document collections. Against a public web-search agent, it answers up to 4.2x more questions correctly, while moving 2.9-41x less data per query. Because retrieval terminates at publisher-operated servers, attribution, provenance, and usage policies travel with the content, realigning incentives across the web ecosystem.

papers.title: Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
papers.summary: The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them. We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.

papers.title: LUTstructions: Fast-Reconfigurable FPGA-Based Instructions
papers.summary: General-purpose processors feature a limited number of instructions based on an instruction set. They can be numerous, such as with vector extensions that include hundreds or thousands of instructions, but this comes at a cost; they are often unable to express arbitrary tasks efficiently. This paper explores the concept of having reconfigurable instructions by incorporating reconfigurable areas in a softcore. It follows a relatively new computing paradigm for seamlessly loading instruction implementation-carrying bitstreams from main memory. The resulting softcore is entirely evaluated on an FPGA, essentially having an FPGA-on-FPGA for the instruction implementations, with no notable operating frequency overhead. This is achieved with a custom FPGA architecture, which is tailored towards low-latency for custom instructions and wide reconfiguration, as well as a soft implementation for the purposes of architectural exploration. All code is open-source to foster further research on reconfigurable instructions.

papers.title: Learning-Based Spectrum Cartography in Low Earth Orbit Satellite Networks: A Survey
papers.summary: Low earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks are emerging as important infrastructure for global connectivity and space-based sensing, while their rapidly varying geometry, heterogeneous measurements, and dynamic propagation environments create challenges for acquiring and exploiting spatial radio information. Spectrum cartography provides a framework for constructing and updating spatial representations of radio conditions from sparse observations. This survey reviews learning-based spectrum cartography for LEO satellite networks from an integrated inference--decision perspective. We organize the literature around three representative task categories: radio map reconstruction, localization and state estimation, and map-informed resource allocation. We further examine the progression from classical interpolation, statistical estimation, and structured optimization toward learning-based approaches that exploit environmental context, relational structure, generative modeling, and adaptive information fusion. Particular attention is given to attention mechanisms for learning query- and context-dependent interactions among irregular observations, while distinguishing learned relevance from calibrated measurement reliability. Representative formulations and illustrative examples clarify these modeling principles. Finally, we synthesize cross-cutting lessons and identify open challenges in uncertainty modeling, generalization, dynamic map updating, scalable inference, realistic evaluation, and tighter coupling between radio-map inference and network decision making.

papers.title: NVIDIA Spectrum-X: Hardware-Accelerated Multiplane Networking for Large-Scale AI Training
papers.summary: As distributed model training scales to span hundreds of thousands of GPUs, scale-out networks face unprecedented performance and efficiency demands. NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet has been designed from the ground up to achieve predictable and stable network performance with high utilization and low latency. This paper presents the Spectrum-X multiplane architecture, which replaces hierarchical depth with topological parallelism, and introduces hardware-accelerated load balancing in NICs and switches as the key architectural approach to provide fast reaction to highly dynamic network conditions at the microsecond timescales that AI training workloads demand. We describe the motivation, design principles, evaluation methodology and performance on state-of-the-art benchmarks, as well as the lessons we learned from deploying and debugging Spectrum-X networks in large-scale systems. Our evaluation highlights production-grade AI infrastructure performance across four core dimensions: 98% of the theoretical line rate with low jitter-free latency; strong cross-tenant isolation for concurrent workloads; robust, capacity-proportional bisection bandwidth and 7% latency increase for 10% fabric link failures; and rapid reaction to host and fabric link flaps during LLM training workloads.

papers.title: 6G: From Connectivity Infrastructure to Guaranteed Digital Services
papers.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) mobile networks offer an opportunity to align network architecture with operator control, verifiable service outcomes, and governed automation. This article develops four complementary contributions. The Control Compact allocates ownership and governance responsibilities through an own-federate-consume taxonomy. The Guarantee Economy proposes six outcome-priced service tiers aligned with IMT-2030 usage scenarios. The Network MCP Platform, the principal contribution, is a conceptual reference architecture that uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agentic workflows to operational tools and telecom execution interfaces under operator-defined governance. Two real-network examples from Rakuten Mobile illustrate MCP-enabled agentic workflows: radio access network (RAN) second-line (L2) support combines diagnosis, remediation, and outcome verification, while IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) availability investigation combines evidence collection, adaptive investigation, and reporting. These examples support operational feasibility; evaluation of the complete platform, and its performance and security properties, remains future work. A separate TM Forum Level 4 assessment corroborates deployed closed-loop autonomy for a scoped RAN energy-optimization scenario. The fourth contribution presents Rakuten Mobile's public standardization position and a phased deployment roadmap. The analysis distinguishes operational records, external assessment evidence, standards-based requirements, and proposed architectural and commercial extensions. It identifies validation requirements for broader deployment and outcome-based service assurance.

papers.title: Foundational Refinement Proofs for EVM Bytecode, at the Price of Tokens
papers.summary: Relating executable code to a high-level model of its behavior has been a central concern of programming-language research for decades. Formally verified compilers, translation validators and certifying compilers address this problem through different trade-offs between proof effort, automation, generality, and the size of the trusted base. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have begun to change the economics of formal verification. Agentic proof development is now capable of producing machine-checked proofs, sometimes unsupervised, at a scale and speed that were previously out of reach. We propose a verification architecture that takes advantage of this shift. An executable obtains a machine-checked proof that it behaves according to a high-level model, independently of the compiler that produced it. The proof is written by an LLM agent. We evaluate the feasibility of this architecture for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). We build EquiVM, a foundational framework in Lean comprising an executable EVM semantics and a formal specification language, Stele, that gives a high-level authoritative model of the bytecode's behavior, but commits to no source language or compilation toolchain. We state what it means for EVM bytecode to refine a Stele spec and we build a proof library to facilitate proof construction. We evaluate the capabilities of frontier LLMs to construct such proofs, as well as the cost of proof production and repair. Our results show that agents prove 35 real production contracts end to end, without modifying their source or bytecode, among them core contracts of Safe, Morpho, Compound and Uniswap protocols, with bytecode of size close to the maximum the EVM allows. Several proofs need only the initial prompt, the rest a handful of human inputs, and existing proofs are repaired in a fraction of the original time when the source or the compiler configuration changes.

papers.title: Noise-aware Verification and Synthesis of Quantum Programs
papers.summary: This work provides a comprehensive framework for noise-aware quantum program analysis, ranging from logical foundations to model checking and automated synthesis. While most research on quantum programming considers an idealized, noise-free semantics for quantum programs, we reason about quantum programs that are executed on real, noisy hardware. We use the error models published by quantum-hardware vendors to give a hardware-dependent semantics to quantum programs. We then present a noise-aware quantum Hoare logic with a relatively complete proof system. We finally use state-space exploration techniques for the hardware-aware verification and synthesis of loop-free quantum programs. In this way, we synthesize optimal, hardware-dependent solutions for parity bit-flip, GHZ state preparation, and other problems that commonly occur as subroutines in larger quantum algorithms. We evaluate our method on all 55 hardware specifications provided by the IBM Qiskit toolkit. Finally, we also show that classical probabilistic branching is needed for optimality in quantum programming.

papers.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
papers.summary: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

papers.title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
papers.summary: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.

papers.title: LLMs are Brittle to Simple Code Transformations: Introducing CETBench - A Benchmark for Code-Equivalence Checking
papers.summary: We study how well LLMs can determine whether two programs are functionally equivalent. This is an important problem because benchmarking code equivalence helps assess LLM capability in tasks such as code rewriting and translation. To this end, we introduce CETBench - Code Equivalence with Transformations Benchmark - built from a repository of programs that may solve the same or different tasks. Each dataset instance is created by sampling a program pair and applying a random sequence of predefined code transformations, yielding either equivalent or non-equivalent pairs. Our analysis shows that even simple transformations cause a significant performance drop in state-of-the-art LLMs on code-equivalence checking. These challenges are further amplified in the cross-lingual setting when comparing programs written in different languages. To remedy this, we present a simple fine-tuning-based approach to boost LLM performance on the transformed pairs of programs. Our approach for dataset generation is generic, supporting cross-lingual equivalence checking, the generation of program pairs with varying difficulty levels, and the application of diverse transformations. In our experiments, we perform ablations over the difficulty level of original programs, as well as the kind of transformations used in generating pairs for equivalence checking. Our analysis presents deep insights into the working of LLMs for the task of code-equivalence, and points to the fact that they may still be far from what could be termed as a semantic understanding of the underlying code.

papers.title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
papers.summary: Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.

papers.title: Online Continual Learning on Intel Loihi 2 via a Co-designed Spiking Neural Network
papers.summary: Edge AI must adapt to new classes and shifting data within a tight power budget, but online continual learning (learning from each sample before the next arrives) is where conventional processors are least efficient: each small update pays a full dispatch at full power. We present CLP-SNN, a spiking architecture that recasts the Continually Learning Prototypes (CLP) algorithm as event-driven neural dynamics: a self-normalizing local rule replaces CLP's global renormalization, prototype allocation becomes novelty-triggered neurogenesis, and correctness-modulated plasticity becomes reward-gated per-neuron metaplasticity. Deployed on Intel Loihi 2 as the first online continual learner on that chip, rehearsal-free CLP-SNN matches Replay and SLDA on OpenLORIS at 1-shot; at 25-shot, it stays within 0.8 percentage points of Replay and 6.2 points below covariance-based SLDA. Each prediction-and-update step on extracted features completes on-chip in 0.33 ms at 0.05 mJ, 7.3x lower latency and 341x lower energy than Replay on a Jetson Orin Nano.

papers.title: Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models often exceed a single accelerator's memory capacity. Offloading experts to host memory creates a severe PCIe I/O bottleneck because data-dependent routing keeps transfers on the critical path. We present Specter, an inference system that uses quantization to combine speculative decoding with expert offloading. Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns. This provides accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage, allowing the runtime to organize expert movement and execution ahead of verification and improve both communication and execution efficiency. Under single-request inference, Specter achieves an average 1.50x (up to 1.88x) speedup in time per output token (TPOT) over the state-of-the-art system. Specter makes memory-constrained, single-GPU MoE inference more practical on commodity hardware. Our code is available at https://github.com/wwwwwf/specter_asplos.

papers.title: Computable Quantification in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
papers.summary: Informal statements of G\"odel's incompleteness theorems often run: "any consistent formal system with arithmetic has true but unprovable statements." That reading assumes a classical notion of truth, under which a universal statement is true as soon as each of its numeral instances is. This paper presents reflective grounded arithmetic (RGA), in which truth is grounded in computation and universal quantification is grounded reflectively: a universal statement is true when the system's own proof search certifies its schematic instance, and false when the system refutes one numeral instance. RGA allows recursive definitions without restriction and proves addition, multiplication and Ackermann's function total as theorems quantified inside the system. RGA is consistent, and it is complete for its own, grounded notion of truth: every well-formed statement that evaluates to true is provable. G\"odel's theorems still hold for RGA, as a companion paper shows. The statements that classical reasoning calls true but unprovable have every numeral instance provable but no certified schematic instance, so they are ungrounded in RGA; read instance by instance, in an $\omega$-semantics for which RGA is also sound, they are true. All results are machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL: soundness and consistency; completeness for grounded truth, open statements included; $\omega$-soundness and $\omega$-consistency; that grounded truth is recursively enumerable and RGA represents exactly the recursively enumerable sets; and $\omega$-incompleteness. The logic is neither classical nor intuitionistic: double negation is eliminable as an entailment, excluded middle fails wherever a statement has no boolean value, RGA has the disjunction and witness properties, and the deduction theorem holds exactly at provably decided hypotheses.

papers.title: FEAST: Federated Shared-Space Training for Resource-Heterogeneous Clients
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) must serve devices with varying computational capabilities. A fixed model cannot suit all devices, while training one model per deployment limit is costly. Federated supernet training instead learns one elastic model with differently sized subnetworks, then deploys a suitable one to each device. When client inference budgets differ, however, parameters exclusive to high-cost subnetworks are reachable by fewer clients. We propose FEAST, a federated shared-space training framework that counters this imbalance by jointly training multiple subnetworks within each client's limit. Budget-tailored sub-supernet routing sends only the relevant supernet portion, and sparse aggregation merges the returned parameter slices. The trained supernet directly serves the subnetworks used during federation and supports post-hoc extraction of additional subnetworks without federated retraining. We further show that independently assigning clients' training-data volumes and inference budgets can distort accuracy--inference-cost comparisons in heterogeneous FL simulations, and introduce a one-parameter $\gamma$-allocation protocol to control this coupling. In our experimental setup, the SuperFedNAS and DeepFedNAS supernet training procedures remain near chance at 25M and reach at most $17.09\%$ at $596$M inference MACs; FEAST reaches $71.06\%$ at $596$M, $2.4$ points above the strongest model-heterogeneous weight-sharing baseline at its largest tier. Across CIFAR-100, CINIC-10, and TinyImageNet-200, FEAST achieves the highest population-averaged accuracy among the evaluated weight-sharing methods when each client receives its largest affordable subnetwork. Sub-supernet routing reduces aggregate model-parameter traffic by $6.8\times$ relative to full-supernet transmission.

papers.title: QwenGyre: An Elastic Reinforcement Learning Framework for Training xLong-Horizon Agents
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly undertake extreme-long (xlong) horizon tasks, where a single execution can span hours, hundreds of model--environment interactions, and nearly 1M tokens per rollout. Applying online reinforcement learning (RL) to such executions poses two fundamental challenges: (1) severe execution variance and prolonged rollout delays cause massive GPU idling; and (2) complex non-linear branching generates massive trajectory redundancy, crippling training efficiency. To address these, we presents QwenGyre, an end-to-end framework for xlong-horizon online RL. QwenGyre elastically reallocates GPUs between rollout and training without interrupting live executions, while its trajectory processor reconstructs branching histories, scores partial progress, and deduplicates redundant paths to bound training costs. Scaled to our flagship model, Qwen~3.8 2.4T, with 700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre yields a 6.0% absolute gain on NL2RepoBench (52.5% $\to$ 58.5%) in 48 steps. Across our evaluations on diverse domains of training datasets, QwenGyre delivers up to $1.85\times$ and $1.78\times$ speedups over Colocate and Async, respectively.

papers.title: TreeWalker: Partial Evaluation for Grouped Tree-Ensemble Inference
papers.summary: Many prediction tasks evaluate a trained tree ensemble on groups of rows that share feature values: discrete-time survival models expand each patient into $G$ time steps, click-through-rate models score every item in a search session, and scenario analyses vary a few inputs while holding the rest fixed. Standard inference treats each row independently and ignores this input-side correlation. We present TreeWalker, which instantiates partial evaluation for grouped tree-ensemble inference: constant features are static, varying features dynamic. TreeWalker walks each tree once per group, partitions a row bitmask at varying splits, and skips empty subtrees via an unsplit shortcut. It reads standard LightGBM and XGBoost models; training is unchanged. We prove a structural work decomposition: per-tree work splits into the constant-projected subtree size $|T_c|$, $G$ leaf writes, and a predicate-mask provisioning cost $Q$. For the trace evaluator, per-row work approaches $(d_v+1)/(d+1)$ as $G \to \infty$, giving asymptotic speedup $1/(1-\bar\rho_G)$. On Intel, TreeWalker is ${\sim}3\times$ faster than a row-independent traversal at the reference model size ($T{=}500$, $L{=}8$; $G{=}16$ for SUPPORT/FLCHAIN and empirical groups for Expedia) and $7.7$--$9.1\times$ faster at $G{=}128$ on the survival datasets; on Arm, $2.5$--$2.9\times$ and $5.5$--$6.0\times$. On a scenario-analysis benchmark it is faster in all $16$ configurations on both machines. For f64 models, outputs match treelite GTIL up to tree-ordering roundoff; for f32 models, TreeWalker's f64 leaf accumulation is closer than native f32 to an exactly rounded reference on every audited row.

papers.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which runs the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head on the device to build a deep chain and uses one SLM pass to add alternative branches. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three runs of each system on Spec-Bench show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.

papers.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.summary: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.

papers.title: A mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
papers.summary: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade, the model built for rumour and adoption spread on social networks, now embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and space are one coupled system, and this feedback, not any tuning, makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than reaching near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a question of percolation. The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, self-limiting drive-release cycle, sandpile-like but non-conservative. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours that foraging biology documents separately emerge together: recruitment to discoveries, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These follow from one least-committal principle, the resource field and the search both as maximum entropy, with Levy search matched to the field's sparsity and recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging appear as one system seen in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. That sparse, clustered field is also the generic one, because resources almost inevitably aggregate, so one untuned rule should recur widely.
